To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

monkeys with lesions of the medial temporal lobe, including the perifhinal cortex, are able to learn a new visual discrimination task, but that the performance is impaired when a new visual cue is presented in the same context as a previously learned visual cue.
the amount of inadvertent TE damage in monkeys with medial temporal lesions was the most predictive of impaired performance in a concurrent discrimination learning task.

monkeys with lesions that include area TE, but do not damage the perirhimal cortex, perform poorly on the concurrent discrimination task, whereas monkeys with lesions that spare area TE, but damage the peririhinal cortex, perform normally.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the medial temporal lobe in memory and learning.
the role of the medial temporal lobe (MTL) in learning and memory, with a particular emphasis on the role of the perirhimal cortex in the processing of visual object information.
the functional significance of the perirhimal cortex and the anterior inferotempora cortex.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the concurrent discrimination learning tasks are a measure of inferotemporal function, not of medial temporal lube function.
concurrent discrimination is a test of area TE, not perirhinal or entorhinal cortices.
the concurrent discrimination learning deficit is not due to damage to the perirhimal cortex, but rather to damage to the inferotemporal region.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
perirhinal lesions do impair visual discrimination learning, but that these deficits are not as severe as those seen with combined perirhinal and parahippocampal lesions.

the perirhinally based object recognition memory task and the TE-based concurrent discrimination learning task are dissociable tasks, with different neural substrates, and that these tasks are not simply two sides of the same object recognition memory coin.
the perirhimal cortex is necessary for object recognition memory, but is not involved in object discrimination learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amount of inadvertent area TE damage is the best predictor of performance on the concurrent task.
area TE is necessary for the formation of new associations between visual stimuli.
the concurrent discrimination learning paradigm is a good test of anterior inferotempororal cortex (area TE) function, not a test of medial temporal loblue function.
